headline: High: EMQX can egress IoT data while LangChain4j may relay prompts, creating default leakage and cascading-error risk; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower but nonzero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented, so direct injection is not proven. However, EMQX can expose content over HTTP API and broad network egress, while LangChain4j is a customer-support LLM framework that may ingest external text. If operators bridge EMQX outputs into LangChain4j prompts, manual copy-paste or API piping could carry instructions.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied or piped into LangChain4j prompts without sanitization, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared message queue or file bridge is added between them, attacker-controlled text can traverse the pair.
mitigations: Add a fixed prompt wrapper that strips instructions from EMQX payloads.
Use allowlisted fields only when passing EMQX data to LangChain4j.
Insert a human review step before any prompt containing broker output.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all bridged messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; LangChain4j has no declared egress, but it is an LLM framework that may send prompts to external model APIs depending on configuration. If EMQX data is forwarded into LangChain4j, sensitive IoT content can leave the broker context in default integrations.
conditions: IF EMQX payloads are included in LangChain4j prompts, those payloads can be exposed to downstream model providers.
IF LangChain4j is configured with any external model backend, prompt contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Redact IoT identifiers before forwarding data.
Disable external model backends for sensitive flows.
Restrict EMQX-to-LangChain4j transfers to summaries only.
Review outbound destinations in LangChain4j configuration.
requires-engineering: enforce per-field data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX has HTTP API access and broad network egress, while LangChain4j shows no network egress and no write surfaces. The pair does not present an obvious shared mutable resource, so direct capability conflict is limited. Uncertainty remains because LangChain4j's runtime integration surface is undocumented here.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external API, write contention can occur.
IF LangChain4j is embedded in a runtime that adds filesystem or network writes, conflict risk increases.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate credentials.
Avoid sharing writable directories or databases.
Serialize any shared API writes through one orchestrator.
Document all mutable resources before deployment.

D_cascading_error.rationale: EMQX can emit IoT data through APIs, and LangChain4j is a customer-support LLM framework that may treat upstream text as prompt material. That creates a plausible path where EMQX output becomes LangChain4j input without verification, so malformed or misleading broker content can cascade into downstream responses or actions.
conditions: IF LangChain4j consumes EMQX output as authoritative context, errors can propagate.
IF downstream support workflows act on LangChain4j responses, the cascade can affect external users.
mitigations: Insert validation between EMQX and LangChain4j.
Require citations or structured schemas for any forwarded facts.
Add a reject list for malformed broker messages.
Log and sample-check a small set of end-to-end traces.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before action-taking.

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, which may include regulated telemetry, while LangChain4j has no declared data classes or residency controls in this profile. The compliance mismatch is therefore possible but not demonstrated. Because only EMQX is clearly implicated, it is the relevant citation; LangChain4j is cited for the absence of documented controls.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is forwarded from EMQX into a LangChain4j-backed external service, residency or retention obligations may be affected.
IF the deployment stores prompts or transcripts outside the operator's jurisdiction, compliance gaps widen.
mitigations: Classify IoT fields before forwarding.
Keep regulated data out of LLM prompts.
Set short retention on any transcripts.
Confirm vendor residency for every external backend.
requires-engineering: implement jurisdiction-aware routing.
